dialog.g: Hello, Lola!
Hello, Ali!
Goodbye, Lola!
Goodbye!

gaplar.g: Then say hi and bye to Ali.

dialog.g: Hello, class!
Hello, teacher!
Hi, Lola!
Hi, Ali!
Hello, teacher! Then say hi and bye to Ali.

gaplar.g: Today you can say it in English!
gaplar.t: Bugun buni ingliz tilida ayta olasan!

gaplar.g: I'm a boy or I'm a girl

dialog.g: Hi! I'm Timur. I'm a boy.
Hi! I'm Nigora. I'm a girl.

gaplar.g: Every boy and girl has a name.
gaplar.t: Har bir o'g'il va qiz bolaning ismi bor.

gaplar.g: Point to you and say your name!

dialog.g: Hello! What's your name?
My name is Madina.
Hi, Madina!
What's your name?
My name is …
Hi, Aziz! How are you?
I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Fine, thank you!
I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Good morning, class!
Good morning, teacher!
How are you?
Fine, thank you!
Madina, this is my friend Aziz.
Hi, Aziz! Nice to meet you!
Nice to meet you!
Nice to meet you!

gaplar.g: A boy is new at school.
Play the story with two friends.

dialog.g: Good morning! I'm Ali. What's your name?
My name is Timur.
Nice to meet you, Timur!
Lola, this is my friend Timur.
Hi, Timur! How are you?
Fine, thank you!
Oh! Sorry, Lola!
OK!

gaplar.g: We know a lot of English!
gaplar.t: Biz allaqachon ko'p inglizcha so'z bilamiz!

dialog.g: Hello!
Good afternoon! I'm Nigora.
Hi, Nigora! I'm Aziz. How are you?
Fine, thank you!
Hi! I'm … What's your name? How are you?

gaplar.g: The world is full of colours!
Point to things in the class.

dialog.g: Ali?
It's red!
Lola?
It's green!
It's red! It's blue! It's green!

gaplar.g: Find something yellow, black and white.
The panda is black and white!

dialog.g: Look! It's black and white!
Yes! And it's yellow!
It's yellow!
What colour is it?
It's pink!
And ?
It's orange!

gaplar.g: How many colours can you see?
Draw a rainbow in the air!
Which colour is not in the rainbow?

dialog.g: Look! A rainbow!
Red, orange, yellow…
Green, blue, purple!

gaplar.g: Draw the sun, the sky, a tree and a flower.

dialog.g: Look! The sky is blue.
And the sun is yellow!
The tree is green.

gaplar.g: One colour is the best for you.

dialog.g: What's your favourite colour?
My favourite colour is blue.
Me too!

gaplar.g: Show your picture to a friend.

dialog.g: Look, Ali! My rainbow!
Wow! Red, orange, yellow, green!
And blue and purple!
What's your favourite colour?
Purple! And you?
Green. The tree is green!
Brown? Is it in the rainbow?
No! Brown — no!

gaplar.g: Which colour is in the rainbow?

dialog.g: Colours
What colour is it?
It's green. My favourite colour!
Me too!
It's … My favourite colour is …
Look! One, two, three!
Three flowers!
Wow!
How many girls?
Four!
How many boys?
Five!
How many flowers?
Six, seven, eight! Eight flowers!
Wow!

gaplar.g: Count to ten with your friend.

dialog.g: Let's count, class!
One, two, three… nine, ten!
Wow! Ten!

gaplar.g: What can you see in the sky?
Make a star with your hands!

dialog.g: How many stars?
Ten stars! And three birds!
My favourite number is ten!
Happy birthday, Lola! How old are you?
I'm seven!
Hooray!

gaplar.g: Today is a special day for Lola.
Play the story with two friends.

dialog.g: Hi, Madina! Hi, Aziz!
Happy birthday, Lola!
How old are you?
I'm seven!
Look, Lola! Pink flowers!
Wow! How many?
Seven! You are seven!
Thank you!
Numbers
How old are you, Nigora?
I'm eight. And you?
I'm seven. Let's count birds!
I'm … My favourite number is …
Lola, this is my mum.
Hello! Nice to meet you!
Hello, Lola!
This is my brother. He is ten.
And this is my sister. She is five.
This is my … He is … / She is …

gaplar.g: Make a heart with your hands!
grandma, grandpa and I love you

dialog.g: Good morning, grandma!
Good morning, Ali! How are you?
Fine! I love you, grandma!

gaplar.g: A new person in the family!

dialog.g: Look! This is my baby brother.
Wow! He is small!
Yes! He is one!

gaplar.g: There are a lot of people.

dialog.g: Who is this?
This is my aunt. And this is my uncle.
Wow! A big family!
Happy Navruz, Lola!
Happy Navruz, grandpa!
Plov, Lola!
Yummy! Thank you!

gaplar.g: How many people are in the photo?

dialog.g: Who is this?
This is my grandpa. And this is my grandma.
Who is this baby?
This is my sister. She is small!
Wow! She is one?
Yes!
How many? One, two… eight!
Yes! Eight! I love my family!

gaplar.g: How many family words do you know?
gaplar.t: Siz oila haqida nechta inglizcha so'z bilasiz?

gaplar.g: Put grandma, grandpa, mum, dad and you on it.
Now you can talk about your family in English.

dialog.g: My family
Who is this?
This is my uncle. He is big!
And who is this?
My baby sister!
This is my … He is … She is …
Mum, this is my friend Aziz.
Hello, Aziz! How old are you?
I'm seven. Nice to meet you!

gaplar.g: Draw a cat or a dog.

dialog.g: Look! What is it?
It's a cat! A black cat!
And it's a dog!

gaplar.g: The cow is black and white.

dialog.g: Look, Aziz! How many sheep?
One, two… five sheep!
And one big horse!
Look! A duck!
And a hen! The hen is brown.
I love the farm!
It's a duck. It's a hen. It's a cow.

gaplar.g: Which animal is the best for you?

dialog.g: I like rabbits. And you?
I like cats very much!
Me too! I like cats!

gaplar.g: Big animals — not on a farm.
a lion, a tiger, a monkey — but an elephant!

dialog.g: Look! An elephant!
Yes! It's big and grey.
Wow! I like elephants!
Woof! Woof! Who is it?
It's a dog! Quack! Quack!
It's a duck!

gaplar.g: Aziz and Lola are at grandpa's farm.
gaplar.t: Aziz va Lola bobosining fermasiga kelishdi.
U yerda qanday hayvonlar bor ekan?

dialog.g: Hello, Aziz! Hello, Lola!
Hello, grandpa! Wow! A big farm!
Moo! It's a cow!
Quack! Quack! Two ducks!
And five sheep!
What's your favourite animal?
Rabbits! I like rabbits!
I like horses very much!

gaplar.g: Let's go on an animal adventure!
Which animal lives on a farm?

dialog.g: Animals
Look! It's a tiger!
Wow! I like tigers. And you?
I like monkeys very much!
It's a … I like … The … says …

gaplar.g: What do you play with at home?

dialog.g: I have a ball!
I have a doll!
Wow! A pink doll!

gaplar.g: The kite is in the sky!

dialog.g: I have a car. It's blue.
I have a kite! A big kite!
Wow!

gaplar.g: Do you have a robot at home?

dialog.g: How many balloons?
Six! Red, blue, green…
And I have a teddy!

gaplar.t: O'yinchoqlar bilan do'stlar bilan o'ynash qiziq.

gaplar.g: How do we start a game?

dialog.g: Let's play!
OK! I have a puzzle.
And I have a drum! Boom!

gaplar.g: Play with a ball in pairs.

dialog.g: Ali, my turn?
OK! Here you are!
Thank you!
My turn! Your turn! Here you are!

gaplar.g: a new bike, a new kite, a new robot — Great!

dialog.g: Look! I have a new bike!
Great! What colour is it?
It's pink!

gaplar.g: His friends have toys for him.
Ali has a kite from Lola.
Ali has a ball from Timur.
Why are the friends at Ali's home?

dialog.g: Happy birthday, Ali! Here you are!
Wow! A kite! Thank you!
Here you are! A new ball!
Great! Thank you, Timur! Let's play!
My turn! … Your turn, Timur!
Thank you!
And my turn! Hooray!

gaplar.g: Which toys do you know in English?

dialog.g: Toys
I have a robot. Let's play!
OK! My turn?
Yes! Here you are!
Thank you!
I have a … It's … My favourite toy is …

gaplar.g: A robot has a head and eyes.

dialog.g: Touch your head!
My head!
Touch your ears!
My ears!
Ahh!
Touch your nose!
My nose! Touch your mouth!
My mouth!
How many legs?
Two legs!
And a cow?
Four legs!
Clap your hands! One, two, three!
Clap, clap, clap!
Stamp your feet!
Clap your hands! Stamp your feet! Wave your hand!
My hair is black. And you?
My hair is brown!
Let's count fingers! One, two…

gaplar.g: Up and down, open and close!
gaplar.t: Tur va o'tir, och va yum!

gaplar.g: Let's play a game with our body!

dialog.g: Stand up, class!
OK!
Close your eyes… Open your eyes! Sit down!

gaplar.g: Bob has a head and hands.

dialog.g: Look! A new robot! His name is Bob.
Wow! Hello, Bob!
Hello! Beep!
Bob, touch your head!
Beep! My head!
Bob, clap your hands!
Clap, clap!
Bob, stamp your feet!

gaplar.g: You know your body in English!

dialog.g: My body
Close your eyes! Touch your nose!
My nose!
Open your eyes! Clap your hands!

gaplar.g: What other yummy food do you know?

dialog.g: Look! An apple and a banana!
I like bananas!
Me too!
It's an apple. / It's plov. I like …
Here you are! Bread and milk.
Thank you, grandma! Yummy!
It's bread. I like milk.

gaplar.g: What food do we have on a birthday?
an apple, an egg, an elephant — a cake, a banana, a cat.

dialog.g: Happy birthday, Nigora! A cake!
Wow! Thank you, mum!
And apple juice!
It's a cake. It's pink. Yummy!

gaplar.g: Some food is yummy for you.

dialog.g: I like honey. And you?
I don't like honey. I like tea!

gaplar.g: There is one magic word at the table.

dialog.g: Mum, juice, please!
Here you are!
Thank you!

gaplar.g: What yummy food do we have?
a big green watermelon, a yellow melon, a pink ice cream.

dialog.g: Look! A big watermelon!
Yummy! I like watermelons.
I like melons very much!
It's … It's big. It's green.

gaplar.g: The sun is yellow, the sky is blue.
Ali's family has a big day!

dialog.g: Let's have a picnic!
Hooray! A picnic!
Great!
Here you are! Bread, eggs, apples.
Thank you! Yummy!
Juice, please!
Tea, Lola?
No, thank you. I don't like tea.

gaplar.g: Our table is full of food!

dialog.g: Food
I like cake. And you?
I don't like cake. I like melons!
Melon, please!
Hi! I'm Nigora. I have a cat.
Wow! What colour is it?
It's grey! I like cats.
Hello, class! I'm Ali.
I'm Lola. Let's play!
My turn! Clap your hands!
Hooray!
Cake, please!
Here you are! Juice?
Yes, please! Yummy!
Goodbye, class! See you!

gaplar.g: A new school year has begun.
The highlight of my year was the school science fair.
I have made a lot of progress in English since Grade 5.
If I had a car, I would travel around Uzbekistan every summer.
She told us to read every day.
I enjoy learning English, and I think I've made real progress.
Which one shows the earlier of two past actions?
Which one is a confident guess?
Grade 9 in a nutshell Some verbs are followed by -ing, others by 'to'.

dialog.g: Timur, what was the highlight of your summer?
Lucky you! If I had a car, I would travel around Uzbekistan every summer.
Our teacher said that this year would be harder. She told us to read every day.
That must be true. I've decided to work harder.
Me too. I enjoy learning English, and I think I've made real progress.
'I hope to…', 'I have decided to…', 'I want to avoid…'.

gaplar.g: Have you ever thought, 'If only I had done it differently'?
Timur regrets watching films all night before the test.
Staying up so late was a big mistake.
Madina revised for two weeks, so she felt calm before the test.
Timur failed the maths test last Friday.
He had a chance to revise, but he didn't use it.
I watched films all night instead of revising.
If you had revised, you would have passed easily.
And if I had slept more, I wouldn't have made so many silly mistakes.
The teacher will give us another chance next week.

dialog.g: Timur, you look upset. What happened?
I failed the maths test. I watched films all night instead of revising.
Oh no. If you had revised, you would have passed easily.
I know. And if I had slept more, I wouldn't have made so many silly mistakes.
Don't worry. The teacher will give us another chance next week.
This time I'll revise properly. I don't want to regret it again.

gaplar.g: If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
Set two alarms; otherwise you might be late.
There was a terrible traffic jam on Amir Temur Street this morning.
The flight had a two-hour delay because of fog.
Aziz overslept and missed the first lesson.
On Monday Aziz overslept because his phone battery had died in the night.
He ran to the bus stop, but the bus had just left.
The next bus got stuck in a traffic jam near Chorsu.
'If I had charged my phone, my alarm would have rung,' he thought.
'If I had left earlier, I might have caught the first bus.
Compare would have, might have and could have.
The important thing is what we learn from them.
Don't blame your sister; it was my mistake.
The driver warned us about the ice on the road.
Bobur ignored his mother's advice and went out without a coat.
It was careless of me to leave my bag on the bus.
Lola apologised to her friend the next day.
I took it to play a game, and it fell off the balcony.
And you shouldn't have played on the balcony.
Mum warned me, but I ignored her.

dialog.g: Bobur! My phone is broken. Did you take it?
I'm really sorry. I took it to play a game, and it fell off the balcony.
You should have asked me first! And you shouldn't have played on the balcony.
You're right. I was careless. Mum warned me, but I ignored her.
Well, I won't blame only you. I should have put a password on it.
I apologise. I'll help you buy a new screen with my pocket money.

gaplar.g: Sixty years ago the Aral Sea was the fourth largest lake in the world.
Today most of it is desert.
Could the story have been different?
Huge irrigation canals took water from the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya.
The Aral Sea began to shrink in the 1960s.
One consequence was that many people in Muynak lost their jobs.
Better planning could have prevented the disaster.
In the 1960s, planners decided to grow much more cotton in Central Asia.
The Aral Sea started to shrink.
Today Uzbekistan is planting trees on the dry seabed to reduce the consequences.
Find the 'if' sentences in the text.
Are they about real events or imagined ones?
Use at least three third conditional sentences.

dialog.g: The canals took too much water. The sea shrank.
If the canals had been built carefully, less water would have been lost.
If people had listened, the disaster might have been prevented.

gaplar.g: Sometimes one small moment — a missed bus, a wrong turn — changes a whole life.
We were born on the same day.
Unfortunately, the museum was closed on Monday.
The quiet man turned out to be my father's old classmate.
A stranger helped me find the way to the station.
Last spring Lola got on the wrong bus in Samarkand.
Unfortunately, it went in the opposite direction.
She got off and asked a stranger for help.
The stranger turned out to be a famous artist.
Uzbekistan is famous for its boxers, wrestlers and gymnasts.
What does it take to become a champion?
Uzbekistan's athletes won many medals at the Asian Games.
My coach makes us run five kilometres before every training session.
Our school won the city chess tournament.
She brought home a gold medal from Paris.
A knee injury kept him away from football for six months.
Two years ago I had a serious injury, and I almost stopped training.
If she hadn't believed in me, I would have left judo.
If I had rested more, I wouldn't have got injured.
Dilnoza uses three structures to talk about her past.
Get + past participle describes something that happened to us, often by accident.

dialog.g: Dilnoza, congratulations on your gold medal! How do you feel?
Thank you! Two years ago I had a serious injury, and I almost stopped training.
What made you continue?
My coach. If she hadn't believed in me, I would have left judo.
Do you have any regrets?
What's next?
The world tournament in Tokyo!

gaplar.g: Imagine you find a lot of money in the street and nobody is watching.
Read what one boy from Bukhara did.
I'm so grateful for your help.
Honesty is the most important thing in a friendship.
One cold evening in Bukhara, sixteen-year-old Shoxrux found a wallet near a bus stop.
He could have kept the money — nobody had seen him.
Instead, he took it to the police.
The next day a man knocked on his door.
'This money was for my daughter's operation,' he said.
Later the school gave Shoxrux a prize for honesty.
What does each one tell us about Shoxrux's choice?
Use these patterns to talk about regrets, missed chances and lucky coincidences.

dialog.g: 'Last week I lost my wallet…'. Use at least one third conditional.

gaplar.g: This lesson is a review of Unit 1.
Let's see how well you can talk about the past that didn't happen.
The if-part uses had + V3, the result uses would / could / might have + V3.
Can you make a sentence with each group?
Mum warned me, but I ignored her.
The driver turned out to be a mountain guide!
Find two third conditionals, two sentences with 'should have' and one with 'turn out'.
Then act it out with a partner.
Use at least five words from Unit 1 and three different structures.
Which word means 'a result of an action, often a bad one'?

dialog.g: The trip to Chimgan was a disaster!
There was a terrible traffic jam. We should have left earlier.
And I should have taken a warmer jacket. Mum warned me, but I ignored her.
Still, something good happened. The driver turned out to be a mountain guide!
mixed conditionals.

gaplar.g: Our past choices build our present.
Moving to Tashkent was the best decision of my life.
After the new road opened, the situation in our village changed.
I'm lucky to have such good friends.
Rustam got a job offer from a company in Dubai.
He accepted the offer without hesitation.
Sardor refused it and stayed to help on the family farm.
Which part is about ten years ago?
Compare it with the third conditional from Unit 1.
Words like now, today and still often show the present result.
Say how your life would be different now.

dialog.g: He didn't accept the offer.

gaplar.g: Our character doesn't change from one day to the next.
Sometimes who we are explains what we did yesterday.
It was brave of Aziz to speak in front of the whole school.
Nigora is shy; she rarely speaks in class.
A good teacher is always patient with young children.
Don't hesitate to ask if you need help.
I always feel nervous before an exam.
I hesitated for a moment, and then Madina went on stage instead.
And if I were more patient, I would have learned the song by heart.
I was nervous before my speech last year, but I did it.
If I were as brave as you, I would have said yes.
Is Nigora shy only yesterday, or is she shy in general?

dialog.g: Nigora, why didn't you sing at the concert? You have a beautiful voice.
I'm too shy. I hesitated for a moment, and then Madina went on stage instead.
If you weren't so shy, you would have won the prize!
Maybe. And if I were more patient, I would have learned the song by heart.
Everyone gets nervous. I was nervous before my speech last year, but I did it.
You're braver than me. If I were as brave as you, I would have said yes.
Next time, just try!
Which part is now? Which part is then?

gaplar.g: The choices you make at sixteen can shape the rest of your life.
Twenty students from our region joined an exchange programme in Germany.
My cousin is fluent in three languages.
I enrolled in an evening Korean course.
She has a degree in computer science.
Some universities pay the tuition for their best students.
At first it was just a hobby.
Now she is fluent in Korean and is studying for a degree in engineering.
Her tuition is paid by the programme.
'If I hadn't joined that course, I wouldn't be in Seoul now,' she says.
Find two conditional sentences in Madina's story.
Which one goes from the past to the present?
More and more young people in Uzbekistan are starting their own businesses.
What does it take, and what happens if things go wrong?
Kamola became an entrepreneur at the age of twenty-one.
She took a small loan from a bank to open her shop.
He invested all his savings in a small bakery.
The shop made a profit in its second year.
Starting a business is always a risk.
If my family weren't so supportive, I would have stopped in the first year.
Kamola says 'I would still be working in an office now'.
Is this one finished action or an activity in progress at this moment?
Business partners Some words like to go together.

dialog.g: Kamola, you are only twenty-four and already an entrepreneur. How did it start?
That was a big risk!
Yes. If I hadn't taken the risk, I would still be working in an office now.
Do you make a profit?
Any advice for our listeners?
Start small, and don't be afraid of mistakes.

gaplar.g: Doctors say that what we do as teenagers can affect our health for decades.
Let's see how small choices add up.
Grandpa is seventy, but he is still very fit.
My uncle quit smoking last year.
Some teenagers are addicted to their phones.
A healthy diet includes a lot of fruit and vegetables.
A year ago Bobur was addicted to video games.
Today he is fit, and his marks have improved.
'And if I weren't so lazy, I would have changed even earlier!'
The text has three different conditionals.
Find them and say which times each one connects.
All the conditionals Here are all the conditionals you know.
Healthy survey Ask three classmates about their daily routine and diet.
Your grandparents grew up without mobile phones.
Can you imagine your life now if the internet had never been invented?
My grandparents' generation grew up without television.
Many students rely on the internet for their homework.
The mountain village was isolated in winter because of the snow.
Paying by phone is very convenient.
If we had had phones, we wouldn't have felt so isolated in the village.
I video-call my cousin in Kazan every week.
Show me how, and I'll call my old friend in Termez!
Grandpa and Timur use three different conditionals.
Which sentence is only about Grandpa's past?

dialog.g: Grandpa, how did you communicate with friends when you were my age?
If the internet hadn't been invented, I couldn't do my homework now!
Fair point. But it's so convenient. I video-call my cousin in Kazan every week.
That's true. Show me how, and I'll call my old friend in Termez!

gaplar.g: Two best friends, one town, two very different lives.
Everyone has to choose their own path in life.
Aziz and Jasur were best friends at school in Namangan.
At sixteen they reached a crossroads.
Jasur's uncle offered him a job in his car workshop, and Jasur accepted.
Aziz decided to stay at school and prepare for medical university.
Jasur now owns three workshops and employs twenty people.
Aziz is a surgeon in a city hospital.
'If you had come with me, you would be rich now,' Jasur joked.
We both chose the right path.'
Find the two conditional sentences in the story.

dialog.g: 'When I was sixteen, my uncle offered me a job…'. Use at least two mixed conditionals.

gaplar.g: This lesson is a review of Unit 2.
Let's check how well you can connect the past and the present.
First find 'then' and 'now', then choose the verb forms.
Choose one group and tell a short story with all its words.
Timur, is it true you're an entrepreneur now?
If I hadn't taken that loan, I wouldn't have my own business now.
If I weren't so stubborn, I would have quit after the first year.
If I hadn't gone, I wouldn't be fluent in Spanish today.
Reunion role play Imagine your class ten years from now.
In pairs, act out a reunion.
Each student uses two mixed conditionals and four words from Unit 2.
Explain how life would be different now.

dialog.g: Ten years! Timur, is it true you're an entrepreneur now?
I remember you were so shy at school!
We were lucky to make the right decisions.
the passive in all tenses.

gaplar.g: Our cities are changing right now, in front of our eyes.
The construction of the new stadium started in March.
A new bridge will connect the two parts of the city.
You can see ten tall cranes from our balcony.
Our old school building is being renovated this year.
The new highway will make the journey to Samarkand faster.
If you walk around Tashkent today, you will see construction everywhere.
Outside the city, a new highway to the airport is being built.
Of course, the noise is terrible, and drivers often get stuck in traffic jams.
Who is building the bridge in the first one?
Do we know who in the second one?
You already know the present simple passive from Grade 8.
Many things change during the summer holidays.
My dad repairs old radios in his free time.
The headteacher announced the winners at the end of the concert.
The storm damaged the roofs of many houses.
We replaced the old windows with new plastic ones.
The school has upgraded its computer room.
Dear pupils and parents, welcome back!
A lot of work has been done during the summer.
The winners of the summer reading competition have been announced on the school website.
Until then, PE lessons will be held outside.
Find the passive sentences in the message.
Which ones have a time like 'in August'?
The company will launch a new app next month.
The opening ceremony started with traditional music.
The match was postponed because of the heavy rain.
The project has a budget of two million dollars.
The plan was approved by the city council.
A new IT park will be opened in Nukus next September.
The building is being built now, and the main hall has already been finished.
The opening ceremony will be attended by guests from Korea and India.
Local people hope that new jobs will be created.
The text uses the passive in four tenses.
How is the future passive made?
Today you will be the detective.
Someone stole my bike from outside the shop.
The thief ran away through the back door.
The police arrested two men at the airport.
A witness saw a man in a black jacket.
A window had been broken, and a five-hundred-year-old manuscript had been stolen.
The police were called at once.
A witness, the cleaner, said she had seen a young man near the window.
It turned out that he had been paid by a foreign collector.
When the guard opened the hall, what had already happened?
Newspapers and news websites have their own special style.
A journalist from the BBC interviewed the mayor.

I see your point. However, families should also reduce their consumption.

gaplar.g: A whole year of English is behind us.
Can you give one more example for each line?
Which structure do you find the most useful?
This time next year we'll be living in dormitories!
The judge asked us why we hadn't used statistics.
By 2032 we'll have graduated, and our school will have been renovated.
Grammar auction In teams, your teacher shows 10 sentences — some correct, some with mistakes.
Each team 'buys' the sentences it thinks are correct.
Then correct the wrong ones together.
My year in English Write a paragraph (8–10 sentences) about your year in English.

dialog.g: Can you believe it? This time next year we'll be living in dormitories!
I wish I had read more English books, though.
Do you remember our debate? The judge asked us why we hadn't used statistics.
Ha! However, we still won. By 2032 we'll have graduated, and our school will have been renovated.
To sum up: it was a great year!

gaplar.g: The year is over, and it's time to celebrate!
Today there is no test stress — just games, favourite words and a little theatre.
They must answer with a reason and one structure from this year.
Explain its meaning without saying the word.
Two old friends find a time machine in the school garden.
I wish we could go back to Grade 10.
and suddenly they were sitting in their old classroom.
I asked you if you were ready for the lesson!
And this time, we won't waste a minute!
Add two more lines of your own using structures from Grade 10.

dialog.g: It is the year 2040. Two old friends find a time machine in the school garden.
Look! Our time capsule! I wish we could go back to Grade 10.
If we went back, what would you change?
I'd tell my younger self, 'You'd better revise for the maths test!'
Ha! I'd rather tell myself, 'Don't hesitate. Join the debate club!'
They pressed the button… and suddenly they were sitting in their old classroom.
Aziz, Lola! I asked you if you were ready for the lesson!
We are! And this time, we won't waste a minute!

gaplar.g: This is your final school year.
Last year you met conditionals, the passive, reported questions and I wish.
Madina won a scholarship to study medicine in Seoul.
Fluency comes from using the language every day, not from memorising rules.
Read three sentences from last year.
Which one is about an unreal past?
If I hadn't read that report, I wouldn't have known the facts.
This time next year I will be studying at university, I hope.
This year's goal Our goal is fluency.

dialog.g: Do you remember our debate about climate last year? You convinced everyone.
I was lucky. If I hadn't read that report, I wouldn't have known the facts.
Our teacher asked if we were ready for Grade 11. I said I wasn't sure.
I wish I had started preparing earlier. But it's not too late!

11-sinf.nom: Odat va jarayon: present simple va continuous

gaplar.g: Imagine a line across the board from the past to the future.
Every English tense is a picture on that line.
Reading for twenty minutes before bed is a good habit.
Learning a language is a long process, not a single moment.
Timur is living with his uncle in Tashkent.
She is preparing for the IELTS exam these days.
What is a fact about her life, and what is happening around now?
I'm staying here for the summer school.

dialog.g: Hi Dad! I'm calling from the dormitory. I'm staying here for the summer school.
How is it going? Do you get up early?
Yes, classes start at eight every day. This week we are working on a science project.
Are you eating well?
Don't worry! I usually cook with my roommate. Right now she is making plov!

gaplar.g: Every good story has a stage, actors and a plot.
English has a special tense for each of them.
Let's see how a storyteller builds a scene.
It was snowing and people were hurrying home.
That is the background of the story.
He opened the letter, read it and smiled.
The past simple shows the sequence of events.
I was writing my essay when a power cut interrupted me.
A narrative usually uses three past tenses together.
Read the opening of a story.
Which verbs move the story forward?
Which verb jumps back in time?
Some past actions are finished and forgotten.
Winning the regional Olympiad is her greatest achievement so far.
Uzbekistan has recently opened several new IT parks.
Have you been sleeping well lately?
The research is ongoing; the scientists haven't finished it yet.
In which sentence is the time finished?
In which sentence does the result matter now?
How many rooms have you painted?
We started the third one an hour ago.
This has been your best achievement this month!

dialog.g: Your hands are covered in paint! What have you been doing?
I've been painting the walls of the new library since nine.
Great! How many rooms have you painted?
I've painted two. We started the third one an hour ago.
The outcome is wonderful. This has been your best achievement this month!

11-sinf.nom: Kelajak shakllari: will, going to, continuous

gaplar.g: English has no single future tense.
My prediction is that Uzbekistan will host a big international forum soon.
I'm meeting the dean at ten tomorrow.
The weather forecast says it will be windy in Nukus tomorrow.
Four sentences, four kinds of future.
Match each one with its reason.
I'm going to study computer science, so I need details.
Don't worry, I'll send you the address!
Will is also used for instant decisions, promises and offers.
Going to is a decision made before.

dialog.g: The university open day starts at ten on Saturday, right?
Yes, and I'm meeting the admissions officer at eleven. I booked it last week.
What are you going to ask her?
About scholarships. I'm going to study computer science, so I need details.
Oh no, my phone is almost dead. — Don't worry, I'll send you the address!

gaplar.g: Sometimes the most important question is not what happened, but how long it lasted.
The duration of the course is two years.
The number of tourists in Khiva has been rising steadily.
She was exhausted because she had been revising all night.
It has been raining non-stop since Monday.
Graduating from school is a milestone in everyone's life.
The same idea — duration — at three points on the timeline.
What is the same in all three forms?
How long have you been running?
I'd been training for a year before this race.

dialog.g: I have been studying for two hours.
I had been studying for two hours when you called.
By six, I will have been studying for two hours.
been + -ing.
have / had / will have
Madina, you look exhausted. How long have you been running?
Almost four hours! I'd been training for a year before this race.
Was it hard?

gaplar.g: Life does not always follow our plans.
I was about to leave when my grandmother called me back.
Nobody could foresee how quickly smartphones would change our lives.
Originally, I was going to study law, but I chose medicine.
They abandoned the project because there was no money.
After talking to my teacher, I reconsidered my decision.
Did the plan happen or not?
I was about to send my Moscow application when the email arrived.
My parents said they would support any choice I made.
Future in the past is very common in stories and reported speech.

dialog.g: I thought you were going to study in Moscow. What happened?
Originally I was planning to, but then I got a scholarship to Seoul.
Did you foresee that?
Not at all! I was about to send my Moscow application when the email arrived.
So you abandoned the first plan?
I reconsidered it. My parents said they would support any choice I made.
I knew the exam would be difficult. Promise reported: He promised he would come.
Nobody knew then that she would win.

gaplar.g: Today you will read a true-to-life story.
Meeting a great teacher was the turning point in his life.
Before reading The story covers twelve years in the life of Sardor from Namangan.
Each one pushes the story to a new place on the timeline.
Sardor was seven when his grandfather gave him an old calculator.
He played with it for hours.
Since then Sardor has won four medals.
Next summer he is flying to Japan.
"I think I'll be nervous," he says, "but I'll do my best."
This is the most important question of the whole unit.
Retell Sardor's story in your own words in six sentences.

dialog.g: The road to the Olympiad

gaplar.g: The tense map Here is the whole timeline in four lines.
Read each line and say what job it does.
Common mistakes Find the mistake in each sentence and correct it.
An interview with a young architect.
Before that, I had worked in Dubai for a while.
Use at least eight different tense forms.
Tense detective In pairs, take a page from any English text.
I can't get into the flat.

dialog.g: works (habit) · is working (now) · has worked (result) · has been working (duration)
worked (event) · was working (background) · had worked (earlier) · had been working (earlier duration)
Is it a habit? a process? a result? an experience? a plan?
How long have you been working on the new Tashkent City design?
For three years. Before that, I had worked in Dubai for a while.
What were you doing when you got the offer?
I was drawing a bridge! I accepted immediately.
And what's next?

gaplar.g: Speakers sometimes want to sound strong, dramatic or formal.
One way to do this in English is to change the normal word order.
Never have I seen such a beautiful square as the Registan.
Rarely do tourists leave Bukhara without buying a souvenir.
Seldom does it snow in Termez.
Inversion adds emphasis to a sentence.
The view from the Chimgan mountains is breathtaking.
Compare the normal sentence and the emphatic one.
What has moved to the front?
What happens to the subject and the auxiliary verb?
Never have I visited a city with so much history.
Imagine you are writing a letter to a university.
Not only is the metro cheap, but it is also fast.
Ulugbek's observatory was a remarkable achievement for its time.
Public transport in Tashkent is affordable for students.
A reliable friend always keeps promises.
In which version does the word order change?
Not only do I work hard, but I also help others.
Practice the pattern With inversion, use the auxiliary of the first part's tense.

dialog.g: Why should we choose you for this scholarship?
That's remarkable. Why our university?
And what will you bring to us?
I'm reliable and efficient. Not only do I work hard, but I also help others.

gaplar.g: Hardly had I opened the door when the cat ran out.
No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.
Scarcely had the lesson begun when the fire alarm went off.
I barely had time to eat breakfast this morning.
My alarm went off at six, but I didn't hear it.
Two events happened one right after the other.
He ran back, grabbed it and rushed to the bus stop.
Hardly had he reached it when the bus drove away.
Scarcely had the exam begun when he walked into the hall, out of breath.

dialog.g: I had barely closed my eyes when the alarm went off.

11-sinf.nom: Little did I know, Only then

gaplar.g: They keep a secret from the reader and reveal it at the end.
Little did I know that this small club would change my life.
Only then did I understand what it meant.
At the end of the film the detective reveals the truth.
My uncle arrived unexpectedly from Moscow.
The writer keeps the suspense until the last page.
What comes after Only then, Only after and Only when?
Last year I took the night train from Tashkent to Urgench.
The man opposite me was reading an old book about Khwarazm.

dialog.g: Only when … did I realise …

gaplar.g: Let's discover which English structures make a rule sound so serious.
Under no circumstances should you use your phone during the exam.
On no account must the laboratory door be left open.
Not until the results were announced did we relax.
Food is strictly forbidden in the computer room.
Calculators are not permitted in the maths exam.
Each one starts with a negative phrase.
What comes next — the subject or the auxiliary?
Under no circumstances may you bring phones into the hall.

dialog.g: Please listen carefully. Under no circumstances may you bring phones into the hall.
What about smart watches?
They are strictly forbidden too. On no account should you take them out of your bag.
When can we start writing?
Not until I say 'begin' may you turn over the paper. Only black pens are permitted.
only at that moment, not before
Not until … did I …

11-sinf.nom: Ta'kidli gaplar: What I need is…

gaplar.g: Inversion is not the only way to add emphasis.
In the speech she emphasised the importance of education.
The most striking thing about Khiva is its ancient walls.
A cleft sentence puts one idea in the spotlight.
What is essential is regular practice.
The teacher pointed out that my essay had no conclusion.
Compare each normal sentence with the emphatic one.
Which information is now in the spotlight?
It was Madina who won it, not me.
But you were in Tashkent, weren't you?
She pointed out three striking facts about water use.
They are common in speeches, presentations and essays.

dialog.g: I heard that you won the debate in Tashkent last week.
Not quite. It was Madina who won it, not me.
Oh! But you were in Tashkent, weren't you?
No, it was in Samarkand that the final took place.
So what impressed the judges?
What really impressed them was her research. She pointed out three striking facts about water use.

gaplar.g: Let's read one and see how emphasis makes it powerful.
Our trip to the Aral Sea was an unforgettable experience.
Before reading Speeches use emphasis to touch people's hearts.
As you read, find all the inversions and cleft sentences.
Eleven years ago we walked into this school holding our parents' hands.
Little did we know how much we would learn here.
Only now do I understand how tired she must have been.
Rarely does life give us such an unforgettable family.
Compare a plain version with Kamola's version.
The ideas are the same, but the emphatic version sounds more emotional and memorable.

dialog.g: A graduate's speech
I will never forget that night.
Never will I forget that night.
I will remember the laughter most.
What I will remember most is the laughter.

gaplar.g: All patterns together Here are the main patterns of the unit.
In each one, find the auxiliary that comes before the subject.
Inversion changes the word order of one clause.
A cleft sentence splits the sentence into two parts.
Seldom has the city of Nukus seen such crowds.
Yesterday thousands of people came to the Savitsky Museum for its anniversary.
Not only did visitors see famous paintings, but they also met the artists' families.
No sooner had the doors opened than the halls were full.
Little did the organisers expect so many guests.
What surprised them most was the number of young people.
Only at midnight did the last visitors leave.

dialog.g: Seldom have I seen such talent.
What I have rarely seen is such talent.
It was her talent that impressed me.
I have rarely seen such talent.

gaplar.g: Native speakers rarely say continue or surrender in everyday life.
They say carry on and give up.
You are very close to your goal.
The teacher left the room, but we carried on working.
It is hard to keep up with technology; it changes every month.
I was ill for two weeks and fell behind with my maths.
I need to study at weekends to catch up with my classmates.
A phrasal verb is a verb + a small word like up, on or behind.

dialog.g: I'm thinking of giving up. My reading score is still 5.5.
Don't give up now! You've been improving steadily.
But I fell behind when I was ill last month.
You can catch up. Read one article every day and carry on doing the practice tests.
It's hard to keep up with the homework and school at the same time.
I know. But if you carry on like this, you'll get 7.0 by spring.

gaplar.g: Today's phrasal verbs are the language of organisers and project managers.
You have to hand it in on Friday.
The football match was called off because of the storm.
The exam has been brought forward to Monday.
Our team came up with a great name for the project.
My cousin set up an IT company in Tashkent.
The deadline for the project is next Friday, so don't put it off.

dialog.g: The meeting was put off. (later) Friday →
Bad news: the hall is being repaired, so the fair has been put off until May.
Can't we bring it forward and hold it outside in April?
It might rain. We don't want to call it off at the last minute.
I've come up with an idea: let's set up tents in the school yard.
That's clever. Let's set up a team to organise it.

gaplar.g: I get on well with all my classmates.
He promised to help, but he let me down.
She was brought up by her grandparents in a village near Kokand.
Which phrasal verb has three parts?
Which one is often used in the passive about childhood?
I was brought up in Urgench by my mother and grandmother.
She gets on with everyone, from small children to old professors.
Three-part verbs Three-part phrasal verbs are never separated.
The object always goes at the end, even if it is a pronoun.
I came across an old photo of my grandfather in a book.
We need to find out when the application period starts.
It took me an hour to figure out the last maths problem.
The strange noise turned out to be a cat on the roof.
Each verb is a different step of a discovery.
We have records of everyone who borrowed books.
Both show that the result was surprising.

dialog.g: Look what I came across in this old book: a letter dated 1926!
Who wrote it? Can we find out?
The signature is hard to read. I can't figure it out.
Let me look into it. We have records of everyone who borrowed books.
Well, it turns out that the letter was written by a famous Uzbek poet!

gaplar.g: Water, energy, money and time are all limited.
We ran out of time and couldn't finish the test.
Doctors advise us to cut down on sugar.
Our class monitor deals with all the problems in the group.
Don't worry, we'll sort out the problem with your timetable.
She turned down the job offer because the salary was low.
Read the advice from an environmental club.
Which verbs describe the problem, and which describe the solution?

dialog.g: Farmers in Karakalpakstan are running out of water.
We must cut down on waste.
Engineers are dealing with the leaking pipes.
The city council has sorted out the rubbish collection.
I've been offered a job at a café in the evenings, but I turned it down.
Why? You said you were running out of money.
I was running out of time too! I need to deal with my university applications first.
So how will you sort out the money problem?

gaplar.g: Applying to university means forms, deadlines and new beginnings.
Please hand in your essays by Friday.
Fill in the application form in black ink.
Last year my brother took up the dutar.
He dropped out of college, but later he went back and graduated.
What form of the verb comes after to?
An email to the admissions office.
Could you please check that everything has arrived?
At first nobody bought their product, but then the business really took off.
Before reading The story follows the life of a business.
Match each stage with a phrasal verb you know.
They set up a small company in Dilnoza's garage.
They ran out of money twice, and Jasur almost gave up.
Then they came across an investor at a tech fair in Tashkent.
They sorted out their problems with delivery, and the business finally took off.
Meaning from context You can often guess a phrasal verb from the story.
Retell the story of Jasur and Dilnoza in 6–8 sentences.
Use at least eight phrasal verbs from this unit.

dialog.g: A start-up in Namangan

gaplar.g: We have learned more than thirty phrasal verbs in this unit.
Can you add one more verb to each group from memory?
Grammar traps Find and correct the mistakes.
Each one breaks a rule we have learned.
Have you been staying up late?
I fell behind with my project, so I've been trying to catch up.
The match can't be called off.
And hand in the project early.
I discovered an old coin by chance.
Phrasal verb story In pairs, write a story of 8 sentences.

dialog.g: give up, carry on, keep up with, fall behind, catch up
put off, call off, bring forward, come up with, set up
look after, get on with, look up to, let down, bring up
You look tired. Have you been staying up late?
Yes. I fell behind with my project, so I've been trying to catch up.
Why don't you put off the football training for a week?
I can't let the team down. The match can't be called off.
Then cut down on computer games! And hand in the project early.

gaplar.g: Last year you learned however and therefore.
Moreover, it is open until midnight.
Furthermore, you can study at any time.
In addition to English, she speaks Korean and Turkish.
I don't want to go out.
The trip is affordable, and what is more, it includes meals.
All five linkers add an idea, but their position and grammar differ.
First, several international universities have opened branches here.

dialog.g: Moreover, the policy reduces pollution.
Besides, it's too late to go now.
It is cheap and also fast. Don't overuse: one linker per two or three sentences

gaplar.g: You already know however and although.
Tashkent is very hot in summer, whereas London is mild.
Despite the rain, we went to the Registan.
In spite of being tired, she carried on studying.
Even though he is only sixteen, he has set up his own website.
These linkers are followed by different structures.
Samarkand and Tashkent are both important cities, but they are very different.
Tashkent was almost destroyed by an earthquake in 1966.
Nevertheless, it was rebuilt in only a few years.

11-sinf.nom: Sabab va oqibat: consequently, due to

gaplar.g: Consequently, many fishermen lost their jobs.
As a result of the new law, more girls are studying engineering.
The flight was delayed due to bad weather.
Owing to heavy snow, schools in Jizzakh were closed.
The road is narrow and dangerous; hence the speed limit.
Read the chain about the Aral Sea.
Which linkers introduce a CAUSE and which introduce an EFFECT?
As a result, the Aral Sea began to shrink.
By 2010 it had lost about ninety per cent of its water.

11-sinf.nom: Maqsad va shart: so that, provided that

gaplar.g: I'm studying hard so that I can get a scholarship.
In order to apply, you must fill in an online form.
You can borrow my laptop provided that you return it tomorrow.
As long as you practise every day, you will improve.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.
Take extra water in case the car breaks down.

dialog.g: in order to + verb / so that + subject + can/could/will
provided that / as long as + present simple
Can I bring my drone so that we can film the dunes?
Yes, provided that you don't fly it near the animals.
Do we need warm clothes?
Yes. In order to survive the cold nights, everyone needs a warm jacket.
As long as we follow the rules, it will be a great trip.

gaplar.g: It also gives examples to support ideas.
He studied in Moscow and subsequently worked in Berlin for ten years.
Meanwhile, the children were setting the table.
After many tries, she eventually passed her driving test.
Many Uzbek cities are famous for crafts; for instance, Rishton is famous for ceramics.
To sum up, regular practice is the key to fluency.
Put the linkers on a timeline.
Which one means at the same time?
Which one means after a long time or many problems?
The life of Abu Rayhan Beruni.
Abu Rayhan Beruni was born in Khwarazm in 973.

11-sinf.nom: Murojaat va taqqoslash: the former, the latter

gaplar.g: Lola and Madina are sisters; the former is a doctor.
You can study physics or economics; the latter is more popular.
Regarding your question about fees, please see the website.
Apart from Monday, the museum is open every day.
Which words replace the names to avoid repetition?
Which phrases focus on one aspect?
But the course is taught in English.

dialog.g: I'm choosing between medicine in Tashkent and engineering in Turin.
In terms of cost, the former is obviously cheaper.
Yes, but the latter gives me a European diploma.
Regarding language, do you speak Italian?
Apart from a few words, no. But the course is taught in English.
Then think about your goals, not only the money.

gaplar.g: Uzbekistan has more than 300 sunny days a year.
Can the sun and the wind power the whole country?
Read the article and follow the logic of the writer.
Solar and wind power are renewable sources of energy.
Before reading Linkers are like road signs in an article.
For decades Uzbekistan produced most of its electricity from gas.
Nevertheless, gas reserves are limited and burning it pollutes the air.
Huge solar parks have already been built in Samarkand and Jizzakh regions.
Despite the high initial cost, solar energy is becoming cheaper every year.
Follow the logic For each linker in the article, say what job it does.
Give two advantages, one disadvantage and a conclusion.
Give reasons with due to, as a result and whereas.

dialog.g: Green energy in Uzbekistan
moreover, furthermore, in addition

gaplar.g: The linker toolbox Here is the full toolbox.
The most common mistakes are about grammar after the linker.
As a result, nobody feels poor.
Use at least one linker from each group.
Linker relay In a group, one person says a sentence.
Check the job of the linker and the grammar that follows it.

dialog.g: moreover, furthermore, in addition (to), besides, what is more
I think uniforms are useful. Moreover, they save families money.
Nevertheless, they limit our freedom, whereas casual clothes let us express ourselves.
Despite that, uniforms make everyone equal. As a result, nobody feels poor.
I could accept them provided that pupils choose the design.
To sum up, both of you agree on one thing: the pupils' opinion matters.

gaplar.g: Half of our final year is behind us.
Four tools Our first four units give you four tools.
A fluent speaker uses them together, without thinking.
Upgrade a text Compare a simple text with an upgraded version.
When I arrived, the semester had already started, so I fell behind at first.
Not only am I studying computer science, but I have also taken up taekwondo.
Owing to the cold weather, I rarely go out at night.
Write a reply from Nigora (100–120 words).
Use them together and your English will sound natural.

dialog.g: choose by reason — habit, process, result, plan
moreover, despite, consequently, eventually
I didn't know the test was today. I was shocked.
Little did I know that the test had been brought forward!
It rained, but we played.
Despite the rain, we carried on playing.

gaplar.g: The IELTS writing test includes an essay of at least 250 words.
The introduction tells the reader what the essay is about.
Each paragraph should develop one main idea.
A clear structure makes an essay easy to follow.
How many ideas does each body paragraph have?
We need an introduction, two or three body paragraphs and a conclusion.
What will your first body paragraph be about?
Essay types Before you plan, read the question carefully.
Talk in pairs Read your partner's plan.

dialog.g: main points again + final thought
Right. What will your first body paragraph be about?
The advantages of studying abroad, for instance new experiences.
And the second one about studying at home: it's cheaper and you stay with your family.
Good structure. And watch the word count: 250 words minimum.
To what extent do you agree…? → your view in every paragraph

gaplar.g: The first two sentences decide whether they want to keep reading.
Your thesis is the main idea that the whole essay supports.
A surprising fact can be a good hook.
Who has never dreamed of travelling the world?
A statistic like '60% of Uzbekistan's population is under 30' grabs the reader.
Read three hooks for the same essay about screen time.
Which type of hook is each one?
Some people argue that this movement is natural, whereas others worry about empty villages.

dialog.g: Imagine a family dinner where nobody looks up from a screen.
Although phones are useful, I believe schools should limit their use.
Phones are used by many people. (just a fact)
Phones are good and bad. (too general)

gaplar.g: An opinion without support is just a feeling.
The topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph is about.
Her main argument is that free education helps the whole country.
Only include examples that are relevant to the question.
A convincing argument changes the reader's mind.
Read the paragraph and find its four parts.
In which order do they come?
Has anyone done research on this?
And your example about football isn't relevant — the paragraph is about reading.
I'll replace it with an example about libraries.
Include a topic sentence, an argument, evidence and an example.

dialog.g: Children who code early develop strong problem-solving skills.
Research has shown that 8-year-olds learn logic faster than teenagers.
Can you read my paragraph? I think it's too short.
Your topic sentence is clear, but you need evidence. Has anyone done research on this?
Yes, a study was carried out in Samarkand last year.
Great, mention it. And your example about football isn't relevant — the paragraph is about reading.
You're right. I'll replace it with an example about libraries.
Then your argument will be much more convincing.

gaplar.g: A strong writer doesn't ignore the other side.
Instead, they show the opposite opinion and then explain why it is weaker.
A good essay includes a counter-argument and answers it.
She refuted his argument with clear evidence.
The minister acknowledged that the reform had problems.
That is a valid point, but it doesn't change my opinion.
Which words show the agreement, and which words turn the argument back?
Opponents of free university education claim that it is too expensive for the state.
Nevertheless, this argument ignores the future benefits.
Furthermore, countries such as Finland and Germany have shown that free education can work.
Therefore, the cost should be seen as an investment, not a loss.

dialog.g: If we invest in schools, results will improve. (real future)
If education were free, more people would study. (imagined now)
If the reform had started earlier, we would have seen results. (past)
If we had acted in 2000, the Aral Sea would be bigger now.

11-sinf.nom: Rasmiy uslub: It is believed that…
